__inputs.name: DS_PROMETHEUS
__inputs.label: Prometheus
__inputs.description: Prometheus-compatible datasource scraping the TP-Link exporter. VictoriaMetrics works through the Prometheus datasource type.

panels.title: Router reachable
panels.description: 1 when the last poll reached the router. Read it beside Web session: a blocked session is not the router being down.

panels.title: Web session
panels.description: The router allows one web session. 1 means a browser holds it, the exporter backed off rather than evicting the user, and the snapshot below is the last one it managed to take.

panels.title: Snapshot age
panels.description: Age of the snapshot every other panel is serving. The poller runs on its own ticker, so this is never zero; well past the poll interval means the router stopped answering.

panels.title: Internet
panels.description: Reachability as the router reports it, not the physical WAN port — that is the link series in the WAN row.

panels.title: WAN uptime
panels.description: Seconds the WAN link has been up. Resets on reconnect, so a sudden drop is a reconnection.

panels.title: Clients online
panels.description: Sum over connection types. When the router does not answer this disappears rather than falling to zero — check Router reachable.

panels.title: Firmware
panels.description: Version string from tplink_firmware_info. The value is always 1; the label carries the fact.

panels.title: VPN tunnels down
panels.description: Outbound tunnels the router reports as not connected. The fallback keeps the panel at 0 instead of empty when every tunnel is up.

panels.title: ARP entries not in the client list
panels.description: The ARP table is wider than the client list: stale addresses stay in it, which is what makes it the place an unknown MAC shows up. A standing non-zero count is normal; the table in Security lists them.

panels.title: Remote management
panels.description: 1 when the router accepts management from the WAN side. Absent, not zero, if that endpoint did not answer.

panels.title: UPnP port mappings
panels.description: Ports devices have opened through UPnP without being asked. Any value above zero is a hole a device punched itself.

panels.title: Firmware versions seen
panels.description: Distinct versions over the dashboard's time range. 1 is steady state; 2 means the firmware changed inside the window.

panels.title: Linked ports below 1 Gbit/s
panels.description: Ports that have a link but negotiated under a gigabit — the usual sign of a bad cable. Dark ports are excluded, they read 0 Mbit/s by definition.

panels.title: WAN throughput
panels.description: The router's own throughput sample, already bytes per second. It is a gauge — rate() over it would be meaningless.

panels.title: WAN link and reachability
panels.description: internet is reachability as the router judges it; link is the physical WAN port. The port can be up while the connection is not.

panels.title: Reported WAN state
panels.description: The raw internet_status string, which tplink_wan_status collapses to 0/1. Useful when the collapse hides a distinction.

panels.title: WAN sample age
panels.description: How old the throughput sample above is, by the router's own stamp. The firmware refreshes it on its own schedule, not ours.

panels.title: CPU and memory
panels.description: Ratios in 0..1, which is what the router reports; the web UI shows them multiplied by 100.

panels.title: CPU per core
panels.description: Core count is probed rather than assumed, so this follows the model.

panels.title: Ethernet ports
panels.description: Speed is the negotiated rate and falls to 0 on a dark port rather than disappearing. Duplex empties when the link drops, which is why it is not a label on the speed series.

panels.title: Wi-Fi radios
panels.description: Channel is the one in use, resolved even when the setting is auto. Transmit power is a level, not a figure in dBm — that is all the firmware reports. The IoT pair is a second set of SSIDs the router keeps for smart-home devices.

panels.title: EasyMesh nodes
panels.description: One row per mesh node, the router itself included. Clients is what that node reports as attached to it.

panels.title: Top 10 clients by traffic rate
panels.description: Derived from the byte counter, which resets on reboot — rate() absorbs that. Numeric client metrics carry mac alone, so the join against tplink_client_info is what supplies a readable name. The join is on (mac, instance), not on (mac): with a second exporter scraped, one MAC finds two matches on the right and the panel errors out instead of drawing.

panels.title: Top talkers, last 24 h
panels.description: Bytes moved over the last day. increase() handles the counter reset a reboot causes; a window shorter than the exporter's history simply reports less. The join is on (mac, instance), not on (mac): with a second exporter scraped, one MAC finds two matches on the right and the panel errors out instead of drawing.

panels.title: Clients online
panels.description: One lane per device. Aggregating away ip leaves a DHCP renewal as a continuous lane instead of two; a gap is the device being off the network, unless Web session shows the poll was blocked.

panels.title: Clients
panels.description: ip and hostname come from tplink_client_info because that is the only series carrying them; everything numeric is joined on mac. Rate is the counter behind the graphs above and misses no bytes; Down and Up are the router's own gauges, averaged over the same five minutes, and carry the direction the counter does not. The gauges are point samples, so the two need not agree.

targets.expr: max by (mac, hostname, ip, iface, type, guest) (tplink_client_info{instance=~"$instance"})

panels.title: Clients by connection type
panels.description: Counted from the client list at poll time. The series disappears when the router does not answer, rather than reading zero.

panels.title: Longest sessions, top 10
panels.description: Session length restarts on reconnect, so a sawtooth here is a device that keeps dropping off. The join is on (mac, instance), not on (mac): with a second exporter scraped, one MAC finds two matches on the right and the panel errors out instead of drawing.

panels.title: DHCP leases
panels.description: A permanent lease has no expiry series at all, so its Expires and Expires in cells are empty — a far-future stand-in would break sorting by soonest. Permanent is its own column and is not the same as being reserved. Sort on Expires in to see what runs out next. A row with no lease at all is a reservation the device has not claimed: its address and name come from the reservation itself.

targets.expr: max by (mac, ip, hostname) (tplink_dhcp_lease_permanent{instance=~"$instance"}) or (max by (mac, ip, hostname) (tplink_dhcp_reservation{instance=~"$instance"}) unless on (mac) max by (mac) (tplink_dhcp_lease_permanent{instance=~"$instance"}))

panels.title: Pool lease time
panels.description: Configured for the pool. Individual leases can differ from it.

panels.title: Permanent leases
panels.description: Leases that never expire, and so carry no expiry series.

panels.title: Reserved addresses
panels.description: Address-to-MAC reservations that are switched on. Not the same as a permanent lease.

panels.title: Leases expiring within 30 min
panels.description: Permanent leases cannot appear here: they have no expiry series to compare.

panels.title: VPN tunnels
panels.description: Outbound tunnels of the router itself. The firmware keeps no byte counter for them, only the current rate, so there is nothing to integrate over time.

panels.title: VPN tunnel throughput
panels.description: Gauges in bytes per second, like the WAN figures. This traffic is also inside the WAN totals.

panels.title: VPN server users
panels.description: Permission to use the router's own VPN server, not an active session — the firmware does not report who is connected.

panels.title: VPN server
panels.description: 1 when the router's own VPN server is switched on. Says nothing about the outbound tunnels above.

panels.title: UPnP
panels.description: Whether devices are allowed to open ports for themselves. The count of ports they actually opened is in the Watchlist.

panels.title: DMZ
panels.description: 1 when a host is exposed to the WAN through the DMZ.

panels.title: Ping from WAN
panels.description: 1 when the router answers ICMP echo from the internet side.

panels.title: Ping from LAN
panels.description: 1 when the router answers ICMP echo from inside. Off makes the gateway look dead to local diagnostics.

panels.title: Port forwarding rules
panels.description: vs is virtual servers, pt is port triggering. Rules configured by hand, as opposed to the UPnP mappings devices opened themselves.

panels.title: ARP entries that are not current clients
panels.description: The ARP table keeps stale addresses the client list has already dropped, which is what makes it the place to spot a MAC that should not be there. An empty Name is an entry the router could not put a name to. Recently departed devices land here too — it is a place to look, not an alarm.

targets.expr: max by (mac, ip, name) (tplink_arp_entry_info{instance=~"$instance"} unless on (mac, instance) tplink_client_info{instance=~"$instance"})

panels.title: Reachability and web session
panels.description: Without these two, a router that stopped answering and a network with no clients on it draw the same graph. The exporter never evicts a browser from the router's single session; it reports the conflict and waits.

panels.title: Exporter faults, last hour
panels.description: tplink_scrape_errors_total carries one series per endpoint that has failed, so it is absent entirely while none has — an empty line here is the healthy reading, not a broken query. Logins suppressed counts attempts held back by the cooldown, the hourly cap or the backoff.

panels.title: Poll duration
panels.description: One poll cycle against the router. Scrapes of this exporter read the last snapshot from memory and never touch the device, so this is driven by the poller's ticker alone.

panels.title: Endpoints failed
panels.description: Endpoints that did not answer in the cycle behind the snapshot now being served. Anything above zero means part of the dashboard is older than the rest.

panels.title: Router clock
panels.description: The router's own wall clock. time() minus this is drift only when the exporter and the router run the same timezone: the firmware reports a TP-Link timezone index, not an offset, so the exporter cannot correct for it and no threshold is set here.

panels.title: Logins since start
panels.description: One login should last. A climbing count means the session keeps being lost — a browser on the web UI, a reboot or an upgrade all read the same from here.

panels.title: Exporter build
panels.description: The exporter's own build, not the router's firmware: the version label of tplink_exporter_build_info. A build made outside a release tag reports dev; the commit is in the revision label.

panels.title: Exporter silence
panels.description: A gap here is the exporter's own silence, not the router's: tplink_up is published whether or not the router answered, while Snapshot age climbs for either. Red is five minutes with no sample, so a silence shorter than that never shows, and the band starts five minutes in — it is the outage less five minutes. It answers for the selector as a whole: one exporter silent among live ones does not show, and an $instance that matches nothing reads red end to end.

panels.title: Buffer depth
panels.description: Snapshot batches waiting in the sender's ring while sends fail. The whole row is push mode only: without -push-url nothing publishes these metrics and every panel here reads No data, which is not the same as zero.

panels.title: Send attempts
panels.description: tplink_push_total counts attempts, not cycles: a cycle sends what it drains from the buffer and then its own batch, so a recovery is one spike of ok, spread over the five minutes the rate covers. While a receiver is down the drain stops at the first batch it cannot send: one failed attempt per cycle, whatever the buffer holds.

panels.title: Batches dropped
panels.description: Batches lost for good over the window shown: evicted from a full buffer, or refused by the receiver. Each one is a hole in every other panel — the snapshot it carried never arrived anywhere. Push mode only: in pull mode this reads No data, not zero.

panels.title: Since a batch was accepted
panels.description: Time since a receiver last accepted a batch, as of the newest data that reached the datasource. One or two intervals is the healthy reading: the snapshot is collected before the send, so each batch carries the previous cycle's success. While sends fail nothing arrives and the number stops rather than climbs — the outage shows in Buffer depth and Send attempts, not here.

list.name: datasource
list.label: Datasource
list.description: Prometheus-compatible source holding the exporter's metrics.

list.name: instance
list.label: Instance
list.description: Exporter instances to draw. One exporter per router, so All is the usual choice.
